How the harmony is made from the vocals

Vocal Harmony Maker turns a mixed song into a second voice in five steps. Only the first uses AI; the others are classic signal-processing methods running in your browser. Knowing what each step does helps you understand when the result is good and when it needs your help.

1. Separating the vocals (AI)

Once a song is mixed, the voice and the instruments are added together into one waveform (two, in stereo), and there is no switch that takes them apart again. Older tricks, such as removing what sits in the center of a stereo mix, also removed the bass and the kick drum and left the reverb of the voice behind. An AI separation model instead estimates what the voice alone must have sounded like.

The app uses Spleeter, a separation tool released by the music streaming service Deezer in 2019, in its two-part version (2stems: vocals and accompaniment). How it works, briefly:

  • The sound is turned into a spectrogram: how strong each frequency is at each moment.
  • For each part, a neural network of the U-Net type (a 12-layer convolutional network: 6 layers that condense the picture and 6 that expand it again) looks at the spectrogram of the mix and estimates a soft mask: for every frequency at every moment, how much of the sound belongs to that part. Deezer trained it on its own internal collections of songs whose separate recordings were available, by comparing the masked mix with the real parts many times over.
  • The app compares the estimates of the two parts, so every frequency at every moment is shared between the vocals and the accompaniment, applies the shares to the mix, and turns the result back into sound.

Spleeter's code and trained models are released under the MIT License, so they can be used in any kind of project. The app uses the version converted to the ONNX format by the open-source speech toolkit sherpa-onnx (Apache License 2.0), and serves it from this site.

The app only needs the vocals, so the two-part model is enough: it is light (about 75 MB) and fast, which matters when it runs on a phone.

2. Beats, tempo, and chords

A harmony note has to fit the chord at that moment, so the app first finds the chords, from the separated accompaniment, where the voice no longer gets in the way:

  • Beats and tempo – the moments where new sounds start, the interval between them that repeats most (autocorrelation), and the chain of beats that fits both best (dynamic programming, after D. Ellis, 2007). This gives the BPM and one cell per beat.
  • Chords – for each beat, the strength of each of the 12 notes (a “chroma”) in the accompaniment, compared with the 24 major and minor chords; the low notes, where the bass plays, help find the root. A hidden Markov model keeps the chords from changing on every beat without reason.
  • Key – the chroma of the whole song compared with the major and minor key profiles of Krumhansl and Kessler, together with how long each possible tonic chord lasts.

3. Following the melody

The pitch of the separated vocals is measured about 40 times a second with the YIN method (de Cheveigné and Kawahara, 2002), which finds how often the waveform repeats itself. The pitch line is then cut into notes where it moves to another semitone; very short notes, such as the slide into a note, are joined to their neighbour.

4. Choosing the harmony notes

For each melody note, the app takes the note a 3rd (or a 5th) above or below in the key of the song, so the interval is sometimes major and sometimes minor, as a singer would sing it. If that note would clash with the chord at that moment, it moves to the nearest chord tone. Notes closer together than a moment are joined into phrases, so the harmony moves smoothly instead of stopping and starting. See upper or lower, 3rd or 5th for what each part sounds like.

5. Moving the voice to the harmony

  • TD-PSOLA (time-domain pitch-synchronous overlap-add) cuts the vocals into pieces one cycle of the voice long and lays them down closer together (higher) or further apart (lower). The length does not change, and the voice keeps its words and much of its character.
  • Pitch correction, like Auto-Tune, then pulls each note onto the exact harmony note: without it, the harmony would copy every slip of the lead singer's pitch.
  • The guide tone is a plain synthesized tone on the same notes, steady and exact.

A key change uses another method, a phase vocoder, which stretches each part in time by the pitch ratio and plays it back at the original length.

Running it all in your browser

  • The browser downloads the model (about 75 MB) once and keeps it. ONNX Runtime Web runs it, on the graphics chip (GPU) through WebGPU when the browser supports it, otherwise on the processor (CPU).
  • The song is processed about 11.9 seconds at a time, so the memory needed stays small even for a long song. Frequencies up to about 16 kHz go through the model (Spleeter's own 16 kHz setting); the very top of the spectrum, where there is mostly cymbal shimmer and air, is kept in the accompaniment.
  • The chords, the melody, the harmony, and the key change are plain JavaScript in background threads (Web Workers), so the page stays responsive.

Your song is never uploaded. Once everything is made, the four parts play together in sync, and the mixer only changes their volumes.

Why it is not perfect

  • Separation leaks. Sounds that share frequencies and timing with the voice — a guitar doubling the melody, backing vocals, reverb — can stay in the vocals, and are then moved with the harmony voice.
  • Chords are estimated as major and minor only; 7ths, tensions, and quick changes can be missed. You can type the right chord.
  • One key for the whole song: a song that changes key partway is treated as one key.
  • Backing vocals in the vocal part can confuse the melody: the app follows one line.
